name: Cervicoplasty / Cervical contouring

lead: Cervicoplasty is a plastic-surgery term for reshaping the neck by working on skin, fat and sometimes muscle. In aesthetic practice it is part of neck rejuvenation and gives a cleaner neck contour and a sharper transition from jaw to neck; the term also appears in burn reconstruction.

Surgeons remove or redistribute fat, tighten tissue and may redrape or excise skin. A 1997 report described a non-excisional approach through a small incision under the chin for patients with good skin contraction, and anatomical work has mapped the neck's fat compartments in cadavers. The literature is technique descriptions and case series.

paras: It is a surgical procedure done by a plastic surgeon, sometimes through a small incision under the chin and sometimes combined with a neck lift. The new contour is visible after swelling settles. Looksmaxxing communities list it among hardmaxxing options for the neck and jaw line.
Operative risks apply, and outcomes depend on skin quality, as described in technique papers. Results vary with how well the skin retracts.

angle.text: Cervicoplasty reshapes neck skin, fat and sometimes muscle to give a cleaner neck contour and a sharper neck-to-jaw transition, and is part of neck rejuvenation in aesthetic surgery. The contour change is visible after healing. Published work is mostly surgeon technique papers and small series.

lead: Cervicoplasty is a plastic-surgery term for contouring the neck by working on the skin, fat and sometimes muscle beneath the chin. In aesthetic practice it is part of neck rejuvenation: the goal is a cleaner, more defined line from the chin and jaw into the neck, and it also appears in reconstruction after burn contractures.[1][2][3]

In appearance communities it is grouped among hardmaxxing procedures aimed at a sharper cervicomental angle, the angle between the underside of the chin and the neck that makes a face and jaw read as lean and defined. Surgeons describe the sagging, banded 'turkey gobbler' neck as one of the most common reasons patients see facial plastic surgeons, and direct cervicoplasty, which removes loose neck skin through an incision in the front, is described as an option for a subset of patients who do not want a full facelift.[4][5] A direct neck lift in men has been the subject of dedicated reviews in 2024 and 2026.[6][7]

The published literature consists of surgeon-described techniques, anatomical studies and case series. A 1997 report described a non-excisional anterior approach through a submental incision without removing skin, for patients with good skin contraction, and a ten-year follow-up was later published. Anatomical research has mapped fat compartments of the neck in cadavers.[8][9][10] No randomized trials of aesthetic cervicoplasty were found.
infobox: Direct (anterior), non-excisional submental, combined with neck lift

paras: A nonexcisional anterior technique uses a 3 to 4 cm incision behind the submental crease, with a thick subcutaneous flap and endoscope-assisted fat removal, in patients whose skin can redrape [8]. A comprehensive approach to neck rejuvenation emphasises analysis of the lower face and deep structures, and notes bone resorption as a component of aging [11]. A 2021 review addressed optimizing outcomes in neck lift surgery [12]. Other papers examine specific fat compartments, including the subplatysmal supramylohyoid fat [13], and lifting methods such as the MACS-lift [14].

Direct cervicoplasty excises loose anterior neck skin, usually through an incision in or near the submental area, and is described in the literature as an alternative to a full rhytidectomy with periauricular incisions, skin undermining and platysmaplasty for people whose complaint is limited to a sagging anterior neck.[4][5] A 2024 chapter on direct neck lift for men reviews incision options and the scars they leave in the anterior neck, noting that submental fullness varies enough that surgeons benefit from knowing several techniques.[6]

Platysmaplasty, which tightens, repositions or supports the platysma muscle, is usually part of a neck lift. As skin loses elasticity the platysma can separate and show vertical bands, and fullness under the chin may come from tissue beneath the muscle rather than from fat alone, so surgeons plan by identifying which layers contribute. Medial repair brings the central muscle edges together; lateral approaches suspend the muscle to the side; and combined methods address both. One cited comparison found medial repair generally more effective for midline deformity.[3][15]

Cervicoplasty has been combined with thin free flaps, such as anterolateral thigh [1] and thoracodorsal artery perforator flaps [2], to reconstruct postburn neck contractures. These are medical reconstruction series, not cosmetic outcomes.

Risks described for neck lift and platysmaplasty include bleeding or hematoma that may need drainage, infection, numbness from disrupted small sensory nerves, temporary weakness of motor nerves that usually improves, and recurrent platysmal bands or persistent fullness under the chin.[3] Over-resection of fat can leave a contour irregularity sometimes called a 'cobra neck' deformity, and procedures that treat the submandibular glands can produce a fluid collection (sialocele) or lower lip weakness.[3] Direct cervicoplasty leaves a scar on the front of the neck, which is a main consideration discussed for the approach.[6][4]

Neck and submental contour is discussed in looksmaxxing circles as part of overall facial harmony, since a defined neck line makes the jaw and chin appear more prominent. It is treated as a surgical option for people whose neck skin or fat is not addressed by weight loss or non-surgical treatments, and it is often discussed together with chin and jaw implants, liposuction and facelifts.

Studies are small surgical series and anatomical work: seven patients with free anterolateral thigh flap and cervicoplasty [1], a cadaver study of ten heads [10], and technique papers [8][11][14]. One registered trial, NCT05515016, tested a fatty flap from the double chin for chin enhancement in ten participants; the registry lists it as completed [16].

A 10-year follow-up of the non-excisional anterior cervicoplasty was published in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery in 2003, and an anatomical study described the subplatysmal supramylohyoid fat compartment.[9][13]

timeline.event: Free thin anterolateral thigh flaps combined with cervicoplasty reported for postburn anterior neck contractures.[1]
Ten-year follow-up of the non-excisional anterior approach published.[9]
